newsitem.title: GERMANY: MG chief says earnings to improve in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: MG chief says earnings to improve in 1996/97.

text.p: Germany's Metallgesellschaft said on Wednesday that a positive performance in the first four months of 1996/97 at the diversified industrial and engineering group boosted chances of dividend pay-outs being resumed.
Management board chairman Kajo Neukirchen told MG's annual shareholders' meeting he expected a return on equity of 12 percent in 1996/97, up from nine percent in 1995/96.
MG has not paid a dividend for three years, since massive losses at the group forced banks to step in and haul MG back from the brink of bankruptcy with a 3.4 billion marks ($2 billion) rescue deal.
In the four months to end-January 31 1997, MG reported pre-tax profits of 38 million marks, up from 33 million marks.
MG's turnover in the first four months increased to 5.9 billion marks, from 4.5 billion marks the previous year, Neukirchen said.
Concentration on core activities meant the group was again in a position to look at new acquisitions, Neukirchen said, and he hoped would help strengthen MG's core businesses.

While the figures suggest MG's economic health is on the upturn, a vocal group of shareholders at the meeting was furious at an out-of-court deal with the man they hold responsible for leading the group to the edge of disaster -- former MG chief Heinz Schimmelbusch.
In the end over 99 percent of shareholders at the meeting passed the resolution accepting a settlement with the disgraced former management board chairman and former finance chief Meinhard Foster.
Originally MG had been looking for damages of 25 million marks, while Schimmelbusch had a 10 million dollar suit against his former employer for damages against his reputation.

Under the terms of the deal, Schimmelbusch will receive a one-off payment of 1.5 million marks outstanding from his period in office, while Foster, who had accepted clear responsibility for the financial problems created at the group, will get 160,000 marks.
Both Schimmelbusch and Foster left MG after billions of losses on risky oil deals in the United States were uncovered.
MG supervisory board chairman, Deutsche Bank's Renaldo Schmitz said that an end to the action would save on a long trial which would be both expensive and time-consuming.
To date, legal proceedings had cost the group 4.3 million marks in Germany and 7.2 million dollars in the United States.

"The guilty ones are going home looking whiter than white," said Herbert Hansen of the German Association for the Protection of Small Shareholders and said it was a black day for share culture in Germany.

Economics professor Ekkehard Wenger said that in deciding to settle with Schimmelbusch, the supervisory board had grabbed onto shareholders' funds "as shamelessly as any dictator grabbed a banana republic."

Large shareholders in Metallgesellschaft include Deutsche Bank with 16.5 percent, Dresdner Bank with 13.5 percent, Kuwait with 13.6 percent, Daimler Benz with five percent and Allianz with four percent.
